summary: For ages 9–11, teach reading a cladogram (the branching tree showing evolutionary relationships) as an active tracing and building skill: find relatedness by tracing branches down to the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) node, not by how near two tips sit on the page. Learners place species by their shared derived characters, trace pairs to their joining node, test that rotating a branch leaves relationships unchanged, and confront the tip-proximity misconception directly.
misconceptions: 'Species closer together on the page are more closely related' — relatedness is set by shared ancestors (nodes), not tip distance.
'A cladogram is a ladder of progress toward more advanced forms' — it shows branching, not ranking; living tips are all equally 'modern'.
'The species at the far right/top is the most evolved' — orientation is arbitrary; nodes can rotate freely.
'Ancestors are the tips' — ancestors are the internal nodes, not the living species at the ends.
'Sharing any trait means close relationship' — only shared DERIVED characters define a clade; shared ancestral traits do not.

activities.title: Build the tree from a character checklist
steps: Use a character matrix or checklist (feathers? teeth? three-toed foot?) and tick which traits a mystery animal has.

Place the animal onto the branch defined by the shared derived characters (newer traits) it has in common with others, so grouping follows those shared derived features, not overall physical resemblance or left-to-right order.
Add a new species to a partially completed cladogram using only its listed features, then explain which shared character justifies its position.
activities.insight: A cladogram is built from shared derived characters: in a simple classroom tree, a marked node shows where a new trait is assumed to have appeared in a common ancestor and been passed on to its descendants (some may later lose it), so species group by shared ancestry evidenced by shared derived features.

activities.title: Trace two tips to their most recent common ancestor
steps: Pick two species (e.g. a shark and a lizard) and trace the lines down each branch until they meet at a node.
State that the meeting node is their most recent common ancestor and that this, not tip nearness, sets how closely related they are.
Given three species, decide which two are most closely related by comparing where each pair's branches join.
activities.insight: Relatedness is read as 'most recent common ancestor', found by tracing branches down to the node where two lines meet — a central tree-reading skill.

activities.title: The trap: nearest tip is not the closest relative
steps: Examine a layout where two animals are drawn right next to each other but their traced lines only meet at the very base of the tree.
Find an animal drawn far across the page whose line meets one of them at a much more recent node.
Decide and explain which animals are actually most closely related, justifying the answer by the branching, not the page position.
activities.insight: Physical closeness of tips on the page does not indicate relatedness; only the recency of the shared ancestor (node) does.

activities.title: Rotate a branch and check what stays the same
steps: Rotate a node so the tips swing to new left-right positions.
Re-trace two previously compared tips and confirm their meeting node — and so their relatedness — is unchanged.
Explain in their own words why rotating a branch, or the left-to-right order of tips, does not change which species are most closely related.
activities.insight: A tree encodes branching order (ancestry), not left-right layout; orientation is arbitrary and rotating at a node preserves all relationships.

checkQuestion: Look at this cladogram of dinosaurs. First: point to the two species that are most closely related and tell me how the diagram shows that. Then: here is a new species with [list of shared features] — add it to the cladogram in the right place and explain why you put it there.
checkAnswer: The two most closely related species are the ones that share the most recent common ancestor — the nearest branching point — NOT necessarily the two drawn side by side. The new species is placed on the branch defined by the features it shares, grouping by shared derived features rather than by physical resemblance or left-to-right order.
